query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing short-range chemical order (SRO) through a tailored heat-treatment in refractory high-entropy alloys increases local lattice distortions that impede edge dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby improving yield strength and stabilizing thermoelastic properties compared to a disordered, as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbTaHfTiZrV0.5) with a predominantly disordered solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat-treatment schedule designed to promote SRO without changing the overall alloy composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service conditions (600°C to near melting temperature) under controlled tensile loading and thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of short-range order and resulting local lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: Increased SRO raises the energy barriers for edge dislocation motion, thereby slowing defect mobility and altering the elastic modulus response with temperature. This mechanism reinforces the yield strength and tailors thermoelastic behavior under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Heat-treated alloys with enhanced SRO will display higher yield strengths, reduced creep rates, and modified temperature-dependent elastic moduli relative to the baseline disordered state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, largely disordered refractory high-entropy alloy state.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to RHEAs with similar compositions and microstructural stability at elevated temperatures (600°C to ~1000°C) under tensile and cyclic thermal loads.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the SRO-induced improvements in yield strength and the specific changes in thermoelastic properties remain to be quantified and may depend on the precise heat-treatment parameters and alloy system used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical RHEA specimens. One set remains in the as-cast, disordered state, while the other set undergoes the designed heat-treatment to enhance SRO. Test both sets in situ under tensile loading and controlled thermal cycling at 600°C to ~1000°C. Use electron diffraction and TEM to quantify the degree of SRO and assess dislocation behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated specimens do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and altered thermoelastic properties (or if dislocation dynamics remain unchanged compared to the as-cast state) under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that enhanced SRO is responsible for the improved performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). In Figure 7, we compared the tensile strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA to that of other RHEAs [,,,,,,,], Ni-based superalloys [,,,], heat-resisting steels [], and refractory metals [] at extreme temperatures, demonstrating the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA’s promise for high-temperature applications. The yield strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was higher in comparison to that of typical RHEAs. When compared to some of the most widely used Ni-based superalloys, the tensile strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was about 400 MPa higher than that of Haynes 230 and a little bit lower than Inconel 618 at the temperature range of RT-1073 K [Figure 5a]. Moreover, when the deformation temperature exceeded 1073 K, the strength of almost all metals and alloys dropped. This was due to the diffusion-controlled deformation mechanism activating above 0.5 to 0.6 Tm and softening the materials as a result []. Therefore, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA not only had a high melting point but also had a high strength without any complicated treatment, which means that it has good prospects for high-temperature applications.

The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. This data article presents the compilation of mechanical properties for 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) reported in the period from 2004 to 2016. The data sheet includes alloy composition, type of microstructures, density, hardness, type of tests to measure the room temperature mechanical properties, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength and Young׳s modulus. For 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs), the yield stress and elongation are given as a function of the testing temperature. The data are stored in a database provided in Supplementary materials, and for practical use they are tabulated in the present paper. The database was used in recent publications by Miracle and Senkov [1], Gorsse et al. [2] and Senkov et al. [3].

To predict the mechanical strengthening like yield strength, edge dislocations have been simulated for random solid-solution HEAs in recent literature. Hybrid MC/MD simulations have proven to be a powerful tool to explore the effects of atomic segregation and SRO on the mechanical properties of MEAs and HEAs. For example, Jian et al. used hybrid MC and MD simulations to investigate the role of lattice distortion (LD) and SRO on the formation and evolution of dislocations in a CoCrNi MEA. These simulations suggested that yield strength was controlled by the strain required to nucleate Shockley partial dislocations; LD lowered this strain, while SRO increased it. The hybrid MC/MD simulations of Li et al. demonstrated that increasing SRO in the CoCrNi MEA increased the ruggedness of the energy landscape, thereby raising barriers to dislocation activity and increasing strength. Short-range ordering in HEAs is more complex than that of MEAs (with the increased number of distinct atomic pairs in HEAs), suggesting that HEAs provide a richer environment for tailoring their orders and microstructures to achieve superior strength and ductility. decision.trend: Early studies on refractory HEAs focused on demonstrating their exceptional high‐temperature strength and stability via microstructural tailoring (e.g., refining grain size and phase engineering). Subsequent work incorporated atomistic simulations and in‐situ diffraction techniques, revealing that local chemical ordering and lattice distortions—unexpectedly influencing the activity of dislocations (in some cases promoting edge dislocation control rather than the typical screw mechanisms)—play a crucial role in their mechanical response. More recent comparisons between different alloy families (for example, those comparing alloys with and without HCP elements) have underscored how modifications in local order alter both slip behavior and potentially influence temperature‐dependent elastic moduli. Yet, these studies stop short of a controlled, systematic variation of short-range order to isolate its direct effects under high-temperature, mechanical loading conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains unproven how fluctuating short-range order and local lattice distortions uniquely govern both the defect mobility (e.g., yield strength, creep resistance) and the thermoelastic behavior (temperature-dependent elastic modulus) in a single, consistent alloy system. A controlled comparative study isolating the degree of short-range order from general compositional complexity is missing.
decision.lever: Apply a tailored heat-treatment schedule to a baseline refractory HEA (e.g., NbTaTiV or CrMoNbV) to systematically vary the degree of short-range chemical order without altering the overall composition. Then perform in-situ mechanical testing (yield strength, dislocation dynamics via microscopy) and thermoelastic measurements (elastic modulus as a function of temperature) under defined high-temperature and load conditions.
decision.why: This approach builds on trends that link local ordering to dislocation behavior and thermoelastic anomalies, while directly isolating the role of short-range order. By comparing a baseline, as-cast, largely disordered state with a heat-treated state having enhanced short-range order, the experiment can test whether variations in local lattice distortions are the governing cause for the observed high-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic responses, precisely addressing the previously identified gap.
